## What You Need to Know

The best fine-mesh strainers are durable and allow you to sift and strain even powdered substances well. They also fit on a wide variety of vessels and are comfortable to handle. We’ve recommended our top choice, the [Rösle Fine Mesh Strainer, 7.9 inches](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B007426KZG?tag=reviewpgstory-20), for over a decade. It’s a stellar performer, straining foods perfectly and yielding the finest-textured soups and purées. Its handle is comfortable to hold, and a large hook allows it to sit securely on bowls and saucepans. Although it is expensive, we think it’s a good investment; it’s remarkably durable, and after many years of use ours look nearly the same as they did when we first bought them.

![](https://res.cloudinary.com/hksqkdlah/image/upload/c_fill,dpr_2.0,f_auto,fl_lossy.progressive.strip_profile,g_faces:auto,q_auto:low,w_340/v1/ATK%20Reviews/2025/Fine-Mesh%20Strainers/Fine_Mesh_Strainer_AoTW)

Looking for a smaller version? Check out our review of [small strainers](https://www.americastestkitchen.com/equipment_reviews/2410-small-strainers).

Fine-mesh strainers are underrated—one of those kitchen tools that you don’t know you want but that turn out to be indispensable once you get one. They’re great for rinsing rice, washing small quantities of herbs or vegetables, sifting flour or powdered sugar, and straining sauces and purées so they are silky-smooth. (If you’ve never eaten a soup that’s been passed through a fine-mesh strainer, prepare to be amazed—the strainer will make even the lowliest [vichyssoise](https://www.americastestkitchen.com/recipes/7124-vichyssoise) feel like something that came out of a Michelin three-star kitchen.)

![](https://res.cloudinary.com/hksqkdlah/image/upload/c_fill,dpr_2.0,f_auto,fl_lossy.progressive.strip_profile,g_faces:auto,q_auto:low,w_226/v1/ATK%20Reviews/2025/Fine-Mesh%20Strainers/STP_FreshJuiceWithoutJuicer_StrainPressSolids-26)![](https://res.cloudinary.com/hksqkdlah/image/upload/c_fill,dpr_2.0,f_auto,fl_lossy.progressive.strip_profile,g_faces:auto,q_auto:low,w_226/v1/ATK%20Reviews/2025/Fine-Mesh%20Strainers/STP_SableBretonTartCranberryCurd_Dusting_72)

We use fine-mesh strainers to strain soups and purees (left) and sift sugar (right) and flour.

Fine-mesh strainers come in a range of sizes, usually defined by the diameter of their baskets. For this review, we focused on models with a basket diameter of about 8 inches, the size we think is most useful for home cooks. (We’ve [reviewed smaller strainers](https://www.americastestkitchen.com/equipment_reviews/2410-small-strainers) separately; they’re great for tiny tasks such as sifting small volumes of powdered sugar or cocoa powder onto cakes or straining lemon juice, tea, or cocktails.)

## What to Look for

* **Truly Fine, Stiff Mesh:** It stands to reason that a fine-mesh strainer should have baskets made from really fine mesh. This ensures that any purées that pass through it, such as the [gazpacho](https://www.americastestkitchen.com/recipes/6061-creamy-gazpacho-andaluz) and [berry coulis](https://www.americastestkitchen.com/recipes/77-berry-coulis) we tested with it, will be ultrasmooth and silky. Very fine mesh also does a better job of holding back any bran when you sift whole-wheat flour, as we often do when making [bread](https://www.americastestkitchen.com/recipes/8048-authentic-baguettes-at-home) (the bran can add bitterness and make your loaves dense). In addition, we preferred that the mesh be relatively stiff. Stiffer mesh held its shape better than loose and floppy mesh and made it easier for us to push purees through with ladles or spatulas.

![A pile of coarse bran sits in the bottom of a fine-mesh strainer](https://res.cloudinary.com/hksqkdlah/image/upload/c_fill,dpr_2.0,f_auto,fl_lossy.progressive.strip_profile,g_faces:auto,q_auto:low,w_226/v1/ATK%20Reviews/2025/Fine-Mesh%20Strainers/SFS_Fine-Mesh-Strainers_Fine-Mesh-Rosle-21)![We see an empty coarser-mesh strainer](https://res.cloudinary.com/hksqkdlah/image/upload/c_fill,dpr_2.0,f_auto,fl_lossy.progressive.strip_profile,g_faces:auto,q_auto:low,w_226/v1/ATK%20Reviews/2025/Fine-Mesh%20Strainers/SFS_Fine-Mesh-Strainers_Coarse-Mesh-Cuisinart-6)

Strainers with very fine mesh (left) make the smoothest purees and sift out more bran from whole-wheat flour (a task we perform when making bread). Strainers with coarse mesh let more fiber and bran pass through (right).

* **Relatively Large, Shallow Baskets:** Although the strainers all had similar diameters across the top of their baskets, the baskets’ capacities varied depending on their shape and depth. We found that models with capacities of about 5.5 cups were ideal and allowed us to strain food in fewer batches. We also liked baskets that had a depth of 3 inches or less; baskets that were deeper sank lower in bowls and pots, sitting in the purees they produced.

* **Wide Pot Hooks:** All fine-mesh strainers come with a pot hook attached to the side of the basket opposite the handle. This feature allows you to rest the strainer on top of a bowl or pot while straining. We vastly preferred models with wide, curved hooks, which let the strainers sit especially securely on top of a variety of vessels.

![A strainer with a large wide hook sits on top of a glass bowl](https://res.cloudinary.com/hksqkdlah/image/upload/c_fill,dpr_2.0,f_auto,fl_lossy.progressive.strip_profile,g_faces:auto,q_auto:low,w_226/v1/ATK%20Reviews/2025/Fine-Mesh%20Strainers/SFS_Fine-Mesh-Strainers_Large-Hook-Rosle-12)![A strainer with a wide flat pot loop sits on top of a glass bowl](https://res.cloudinary.com/hksqkdlah/image/upload/c_fill,dpr_2.0,f_auto,fl_lossy.progressive.strip_profile,g_faces:auto,q_auto:low,w_226/v1/ATK%20Reviews/2025/Fine-Mesh%20Strainers/SFS_Fine-Mesh-Strainers_Large-Flat-Hook-All-Clad-5)![A strainer with a tiny loop sits on top of a glass bowl](https://res.cloudinary.com/hksqkdlah/image/upload/c_fill,dpr_2.0,f_auto,fl_lossy.progressive.strip_profile,g_faces:auto,q_auto:low,w_226/v1/ATK%20Reviews/2025/Fine-Mesh%20Strainers/SFS_Fine-Mesh-Strainers_Small-Hook-OXO-3)

Our favorite models had wide pot hooks (left) that gripped the sides of vessels, providing stability as we strained purees. Flat (middle) and small loops (left) just sat on top of vessels, providing no such security.

* **Comfortable Handles:** We liked models with rounded handles that were comfortable to hold for long periods. Bonus points went to strainers with grippy materials on the handle, which made them especially easy to hold, even when wet.

* **Solid Construction:** In addition to having stiff mesh, the best models were also impervious to other kinds of damage and stayed intact when we banged them against a counter 10 times to simulate accidental drops or other impact.

## What to Avoid

* **Coarse Mesh:** Coarser mesh produces coarser, grittier purees; the coarsest models we tested strained out less vegetable fiber from gazpacho and fewer seeds from berry coulis. The coarse, loose weave of these strainers also let all the bran pass through when we sifted whole-wheat flour.

* **Floppy Mesh:** Flexible, floppy mesh sometimes deformed when we pressed on it with ladles and spatulas and warped or detached when we suspended a 12-pound mortar in each model to simulate long-term use.

![A fine-mesh strainer with a deformed, lumpy-looking basket and a red x in the bottom left corner.](https://res.cloudinary.com/hksqkdlah/image/upload/c_fill,dpr_2.0,f_auto,fl_lossy.progressive.strip_profile,g_faces:auto,q_auto:low,w_226/v1/ATK%20Reviews/2025/Fine-Mesh%20Strainers/SFS_Fine-Mesh-Strainers_Distorted-vs-Stiff-Mesh-3)![A fine-mesh strainer with a round, intact basket and a green x in the bottom left corner.](https://res.cloudinary.com/hksqkdlah/image/upload/c_fill,dpr_2.0,f_auto,fl_lossy.progressive.strip_profile,g_faces:auto,q_auto:low,w_226/v1/ATK%20Reviews/2025/Fine-Mesh%20Strainers/SFS_Fine-Mesh-Strainers_Distorted-vs-Stiff-Mesh-5)

Strainers with floppy mesh (left) deformed easily over time, while strainers with more rigid mesh kept their shape.

* **Small or Flat Pot Hooks:** These made the strainers harder to stabilize on pots and pans, causing the models to rock back and forth when we pressed ladles or spatulas into them as we strained foods.

* **Wire Loop Handles:** We found these uncomfortable to grip for long periods, as when straining soups and coulis.

* **Poor Construction:** Several models had handles or hooks that flew off when we subjected them to harsh treatment. While these models might be fine if you were careful, we preferred those that held up better under pressure.

How We Tested

**The Tests**

* Strain [Creamy Gazpacho Andaluz](https://www.americastestkitchen.com/recipes/6061-creamy-gazpacho-andaluz)
* Strain [Berry Coulis](https://www.americastestkitchen.com/recipes/77-berry-coulis)
* Sift bran from 1 cup of flour
* Wash 10 times as directed by manufacturer
* Bang each model on counter 10 times; note damage
* Suspend mortar in strainer for half hour; note damage

**How We Rated**

* **Durability:** We evaluated how well each strainer resisted warping and breakage.
* **Ease of Use:** We rated each strainer on how securely it sat on different pieces of cookware and bowls and how easy it was to handle.
* **Performance:** We evaluated each strainer’s ability to sift bran and make smooth purees.

## FAQs

What’s the best way to clean a fine-mesh strainer?

Quickly. While most of the models we’ve tested can go in the dishwasher, we recommend washing your strainer by hand using soap and hot water as soon as you can after use. (The exception is if you’ve been using your strainer to sift flour; use soap and cold water there, as hot water can gel the starch and make it harder to remove from the mesh.) This keeps any food from drying or caking onto the mesh and forming a layer of impenetrable gunk. If you aren’t able to get to your strainer right away and the dreaded layer of gunk does form, try soaking it in a large bowl of hot water before cleaning. This will help dissolve some of the debris and reduce your scrubbing time.

### Straight to the Point

The winning [Rösle Stainless Steel Round Handle Kitchen Strainer](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B007426KZG?tag=seriouseats-onsite-prod-20&ascsubtag=5509281%7C%7C%7C%7C%7C%7Cpc) is a longtime Serious Eats favorite. It has a deep, generous basket and super fine mesh. The more affordable [OXO Good Grips 8-Inch Double Rod Strainer](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B00004OCLX?tag=seriouseats-onsite-prod-20&ascsubtag=5509281%7C%7C%7C%7C%7C%7Cpc) was a close runner-up, with a grippy handle, sturdy construction, and unbeatable price tag.

A fine-mesh strainer is one of those indispensable kitchen items that no other tool can fully replace; if you ever plan on making homemade broth or smooth custards, you’re going to need one. A strainer is good for plenty of other tasks, too, like sifting dry ingredients and rinsing off fruit and vegetables. But perhaps the greatest benefit of a strainer comes when you least expect it—when you find yourself with a lumpy sauce or an overcooked curd, a great strainer can make it smooth again. In essence, having a good strainer is like taking out an insurance policy on your cooking.

A tightly woven mesh is key, but other elements make the difference between a bad strainer and a great one. I put 10 popular models to the test—sifting bran from whole wheat flour, straining seeds from strawberry sauce, and sieving lumps from thick, pudding-like pastry cream—to find the strainers that are worth your hard-earned dollars. The best ones had more than just super-fine mesh.

## The Tests

* **Whole Wheat Flour Test:** I used each strainer to sift five ounces of [Bob’s Red Mill whole wheat flour](https://www.amazon.com/Bobs-Red-Mill-Organic-Flour/dp/B000YFB5NC?tag=seriouseats-onsite-prod-20&ascsubtag=5509281%7C%7C%7C%7C%7C%7Cpc), measuring how much coarse bran was left behind. I measured the bran in grams and teaspoons to find out how fine each strainer’s mesh truly was.
* **Strawberry Sauce Test:** I used each strainer to sieve the seeds out of a puréed strawberry sauce. I observed how smooth the sauce was after straining, noting how many seeds were left behind in the strainer, or if any slipped through the mesh into the sauce.
* **Durability Test:** I firmly whacked each strainer against the rim of a plastic trash can to mimic the action of releasing debris from the basket before washing. I noted any dings, dents, or scratches, then washed each strainer at least twice, running dishwasher-safe models through the dishwasher. After washing, I noted any visible signs of wear.
* **Pastry Cream Test (Winners Only):** I made an overcooked, slightly curdled pastry cream and used the winning strainers to strain out the lumps of cooked egg. I observed if the pastry cream was smooth after sieving and noted if there were any bits of egg stuck behind in the strainer.

![All-Clad Stainless-Steel Strainer, Set of 3 on a marbled surface]()

The All-Clad Strainer had the finest mesh of the bunch.


Serious Eats / Zola Gregory

It’s no surprise that a finer mesh is best when it comes to a fine-mesh strainer (it’s in the name, after all). A strainer’s job is to remove all the bits– seeds, lumps, and clumps– from whatever it is that needs sieving, and a finer mesh will always do a better job. The whole wheat flour test proved to be the best method for determining how fine each strainer’s mesh actually was. All of my favorites sifted out at least an eighth of a teaspoon of bran from five ounces of flour. The winning [Rösle](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B007426KZG?tag=seriouseats-onsite-prod-20&ascsubtag=5509281%7C%7C%7C%7C%7C%7Cpc) model sifted out a solid half teaspoon of bran, while the [All-Clad](https://www.williams-sonoma.com/products/all-clad-stainless-steel-strainer-set/) (another favorite) sifted out even more, nearly a teaspoon—meaning it had the finest mesh of all the winners.

During the strawberry sauce test, all of my favorite strainers performed equally well, sieving out the seeds and leaving behind a smooth sauce. This showed me that while a fine mesh is important, after a certain point, ultra-fineness doesn’t make a huge difference for most straining applications—that is, unless you’re regularly sifting bran from whole wheat flour (most people aren’t). That said, I also tried several stainers with mesh that were simply not fine enough. Both the [Farberware](https://www.amazon.com/Farberware-Professional-Strainers-Incudes-Medium/dp/B0CTD34L9G?tag=seriouseats-onsite-prod-20&ascsubtag=5509281%7C%7C%7C%7C%7C%7Cpc) and the [OXO Good Grips](https://www.oxo.com/oxo-good-grips-3-piece-strainer-set.html) strainer sets had mesh with such large holes that even whole seeds could pass straight through. When it came time for washing, I even found seeds stuck inside the mesh.

### A Deeper, Generously-Sized Basket Makes a Difference

![A person sifting a yellow liquid through the Rösle Stainless Steel Round Handle Kitchen Strainer into a glass bowl in a kitchen setting with an apron visible]()

Deeper baskets resulted in faster straining.


Serious Eats / Zola Gregory

A strainer that’s too small simply isn’t practical for many everyday tasks, such as straining an entire batch of pastry cream or sifting a large amount of flour. Most of the strainers I tried had a diameter of between six and seven inches. The winning Rösle model was right in that range but stood out for its impressively deep basket. The depth translated to extra surface area for straining as well as increased volume, meaning you could strain more material faster. Another winner, the All-Clad strainer, was a bit shallower, but I appreciated its larger diameter (eight inches), which also made for quick, easy straining.

### A Comfortable Handle Is Key to Fuss-Free Straining

![Hand sifting flour through the KitchenAid Classic Strainer on a marble surface]()

The rounded, grippy handle on the OXO strainer was the comfiest I tried.


Serious Eats / Zola Gregory

While most products benefit from a comfortable handle, it’s a particularly important feature for a fine-mesh strainer. While one hand presses material through the sieve—usually with a flexible spatula— the other hand must support the weight of the strainer. A poorly designed handle can make this task uncomfortable at best and downright painful at worst. I strongly preferred rounded handles, like those of the Rösle and OXO Good Grips models. The Farberware, on the other hand, had a handle made from a simple loop of metal; it felt unsteady in my hand and tricky to grip when full and heavy. It’s worth mentioning that the OXO strainer had my favorite handle of the bunch—not only was it rounded, but it was also made from a grippy plastic that was extra comfortable to hold.

### A Generous Bowl Hook Provides Stability

![OXO Good Grips 8-Inch Double Rod Strainer with red fruit puree being pressed through using a spatula surrounded by containers]()

When you're pressing anything through a fine mesh strainer, a hook keeps the strainer steady on a bowl.


Serious Eats / Zola Gregory

When a strainer is particularly full and/or heavy, it’s nice to be able to rest it on the edge of a [mixing bowl](https://www.seriouseats.com/equipment-the-best-mixing-bowls-how-to-buy) for extra support. All the strainers I tested featured a bowl hook to make this easier, but some designs proved more effective than others. The [KitchenAid](https://www.amazon.com/KitchenAid-KE161OHOBA-Classic-Strainer-7-Inch/dp/B07ZLGG13B?tag=seriouseats-onsite-prod-20&ascsubtag=5509281%7C%7C%7C%7C%7C%7Cpc) and Rösle models feature large, curved bowl hooks, which allow the strainers to rest easily on the edge of the bowl without sliding around. The All-Clad strainers have a large bowl hook too, except it was flat rather than curved and didn’t feel quite as stable. The Farberware strainer set had my least favorite bowl hook design: a small, flat triangle that allowed the strainer to shift and slide during use.

### A Couple of High-Performing Strainers Didn’t Make the Winning List

![A strainer over a mixing bowl next to a bowl of sifted flour on a countertop]()

While most of the strainers were good, there were a few finicky things that prevented them from being great.


Serious Eats / Zola Gregory

A few of the models I tried had super fine mesh, but didn’t make the winners list because of other deal-breaking issues. The [Norpro](https://www.amazon.com/Norpro-2156-Stainless-Double-Strainer/dp/B00004RDE1?tag=seriouseats-onsite-prod-20&ascsubtag=5509281%7C%7C%7C%7C%7C%7Cpc) strainer aced the whole wheat flour test with flying colors, sifting a whopping two teaspoons of bran from the flour. This affordable strainer featured a double layer of mesh that worked incredibly well at preventing bits from coming through. Unfortunately, it was nearly impossible to clean, as debris got stuck between the layers of mesh. The [Williams Sonoma](https://www.williams-sonoma.com/products/williams-sonoma-stainless-steel-strainer/) stainless steel strainer also impressed me, coming in second place for the whole wheat flour test, sifting out a full teaspoon of bran and producing a smooth and silky strawberry sauce—plus it had a deep, sturdy basket *and* a comfy handle. But after just one cycle in the dishwasher, a small patch of rust developed on the mesh, which was especially disappointing given the hefty price tag (and the fact that it’s marketed as dishwasher-safe).

## The Criteria: What to Look for in a Fine-Mesh Strainer

![a fine-mesh strainer with strawberry sauce straining through it into a glass bowl]()

Serious Eats / Zola Gregory

The best fine-mesh strainers have generously sized baskets with a fine weave. My top picks were able to catch at least an eighth of a teaspoon of bran from the whole wheat flour and didn’t let a single seed pass through while straining strawberry sauce. A comfortable handle and a wide, steady bowl hook were also key to easy, fuss-free straining.

Well priced, good-looking, and long-lasting, these colanders are attractive enough to display on most any table. The set features colanders in three sizes (all with micro-size perforations that rival the fine mesh of a strainer) and comes from a brand that Wirecutter also recommends for its pots and pans.

[Buying options: $60 from Amazon, opens in a new tab](https://www.nytimes.com/wirecutter/out/affiliate/v1/Amazon/81361/239177/4/callout/cefef8332ab6461fa6322475714585e1/7)

I still remember the first time I laid eyes on this set — it was nearly 10 years ago in a beach-house rental. (Tramontina debuted the set in 2017.) The place and most of its contents were a bit ramshackle, so when I spotted the colanders in a cupboard while making dinner one night, it was like finding a diamond in the rough.

![](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/05/13/wirecutter/WILI-TRAMONTINA-COLANDER-SET/WILI-TRAMONTINA-COLANDER-SET-superJumbo.jpg?width=150&quality=20&crop=2048:1366&auto=webp)![Three different Tramontina colanders stacked within each other on display.]()

With a gleaming, modern look, these colanders can be incorporated into all kinds of casual table settings when entertaining. When not in use, they don’t take up much space in my cabinets since they compactly nest into one another. Rose Maura Lorre/NYT Wirecutter

I also felt a little jealous: Who knew colanders could look this lovely? How come this seaside shanty has such nice colanders and my perfectly decent primary residence does not?

Tramontina is a [115-year-old brand](https://global.tramontina.com/en/our-story) whose pots and pans are frequently named among Wirecutter’s kitchen picks. Currently, we recommend several of Tramontina’s [nonstick pans](https://www.nytimes.com/wirecutter/reviews/best-nonstick-pan/) and [cookware sets](https://www.nytimes.com/wirecutter/reviews/best-cookware-set/), and, in fact, our kitchen team uses these very same colanders in Wirecutter’s test kitchen.

After that beach trip, I went home and bought myself the Tramontina three-piece set, which includes 1.25-quart, 2.5-quart, and 4.5-quart colanders that nest into one another for space-saving storage. (They’re not sold separately, FYI.) I always know where to find them in one of my kitchen’s lower cabinets, which makes it supremely easy to reach for one in those chaotic moments when I’m in the middle of cooking dinner and need a second (or third) colander — often immediately.

I know I’m rhapsodizing here, and I recognize that a humble colander, of course, is just a bowl with holes that sits there as water passes through. But thanks to its thoughtful features, Tramontina colanders go above and beyond this straightforward call of duty.

In fact, these colanders’ holes are so minuscule, they can easily double as fine mesh strainers. Even super-thin pasta shapes (like angel hair) don’t slip out. And unlike most strainers, these have an inch-high base so that they stand upright in your sink, which is more useful when I’m in the heat of cooking and don’t have a free hand. Even better, there’s less chance of your just-cooked food coming in contact with the bottom of your sink (gross).

They’re ideal for draining freshly cooked rice and pasta or rinsing fruits and veggies, but I find all sorts of other excuses to use them, too. I rely on them when making tuna salad or its vegetarian cousin, [chickpea salad](https://cooking.nytimes.com/recipes/1022291-chickpea-salad-sandwich?q=chickpea%20salad); using a potato masher, I smush all of the ingredients together inside a colander to press out excess moisture and yield that just-right consistency. (I place a dinner plate underneath to catch the drippings.) I also strain my homemade vegetable broth through a Tramontina colander because its holes are small enough to trap loose bits of garlic skin and because I never remember to buy cheesecloth.

![](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/05/13/wirecutter/WILI-TRAMONTINA-COLANDER-SET-02/WILI-TRAMONTINA-COLANDER-SET-02-superJumbo.jpg?width=150&quality=20&crop=2048:1365&auto=webp)![A metal Tramontinas colander displayed next to a OXO plastic colander.]()

Before I bought my Tramontina colanders, this 3-quart OXO plastic colander (left) was the only colander in my kitchen. I can’t remember the last time I reached for it. The round base of the Tramontina colander (right), in 4.5-quart size, is more steady and secure than the OXO model’s thin feet; it’s also just lovelier to look at. Rose Maura Lorre/NYT Wirecutter

Even if these babies weren’t so versatile, I’d still love them just for their appearance. With curved handles, a sleek base, and tiny perforations, these are not your grandma’s wobbly, dented colanders. They’re made with [18/8 stainless steel](https://www.nytimes.com/wirecutter/guides/buying-flatware/) (translation: iron blended with roughly 18% chromium and 8% nickel), which gives them durable heft and makes them less prone to corrosion, according to kitchen editor Marilyn Ong.

They look delightfully right at home among other servingware at a casual meal or party. I’ve used them to serve chips and popcorn (I recommend using a napkin as a liner to catch chip dust) as well as fruit and (undressed) salad, where they can go straight from a rinse in the sink to the table with just a few solid shakes to get the water out first. And the colanders look pretty much as alluring as they did on the day they arrived. When I asked Marilyn about the colanders in our test kitchen, she confirmed that “they do still look completely new after 6 or 7 years” (with the caveat that they don’t get used every day, or even every week, the way they might at home). As a bonus, even the largest one easily fits in the bottom rack of my dishwasher.

I’m not going to mince words here: It’s probably time to upgrade your mesh strainer situation.

Most home cooks have an old mesh strainer kicking around in their cupboards, which gets unearthed for a handful of hyper-specific tasks. You likely use yours to [rinse the sludge off canned beans](https://www.thekitchn.com/canned-beans-foam-safe-to-eat-explained-261489). If you regularly cook [rice or other grains](https://www.thekitchn.com/yes-you-should-be-rinsing-your-rice-228083), you may also reach for your strainer to rinse (or strain) those, too.

But if you invest in [a set of differently sized mesh strainers](https://www.amazon.com/Premium-Fine-Mesh-Strainers-Eco-Friendly/dp/B07G7DM41X/ref=asc_df_B07G7DM41X/?asc_campaign=KT-23214341&asc_refurl=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.thekitchn.com%2Ffine-mesh-strainer-set-uses-23214341&asc_source=%7BREFERRAL_SOURCE%7D&tag=kitchn-20), this one specifically, you’ll suddenly find yourself using them for just about *everything* in the kitchen. You may even wonder why you waited so long to get them in the first place.

[Proto Future Strainer Set

$30](https://www.amazon.com/Premium-Fine-Mesh-Strainers-Eco-Friendly/dp/B07G7DM41X/ref=asc_df_B07G7DM41X/?asc_campaign=KT-23214341&asc_refurl=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.thekitchn.com%2Ffine-mesh-strainer-set-uses-23214341&asc_source=%7BREFERRAL_SOURCE%7D&tag=kitchn-20)[Buy at Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/Premium-Fine-Mesh-Strainers-Eco-Friendly/dp/B07G7DM41X/ref=asc_df_B07G7DM41X/?asc_campaign=KT-23214341&asc_refurl=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.thekitchn.com%2Ffine-mesh-strainer-set-uses-23214341&asc_source=%7BREFERRAL_SOURCE%7D&tag=kitchn-20)

Get a set like the one above and the smallest strainer, measuring around 3 inches in diameter, can be used for fiddly things: I use mine all the time for catching seeds after [juicing lemons](https://www.thekitchn.com/best-way-to-juice-lemons-23051867). It’s also handy for straining stock, or transferring rendered bacon fat or clarified butter into jars (just place the strainer over a funnel). You can use it to dust a baked good with powdered sugar. And my tiny strainer has even replaced the infuser for my afternoon pots of tea.

The medium-sized strainer, at 5.5 inches wide, is what’s likely already in your toolkit. This is the workhorse of your daily kitchen tasks: Strain beans! Rinse a portion of rice! [Strain eggy bits from a custard](https://www.thekitchn.com/how-to-make-vanilla-ice-cream-221812)! This strainer is just big enough to be perfectly useful, but not so unwieldy that it’s awkward to maneuver with one hand.

Big strainers, measuring 8 inches, can be used just like a colander. Mine is often put to work draining pasta or rinsing greens, like kale, before cooking. A large strainer is much handier to grab than the bulky colander buried beneath my mixing bowls. Not to mention, it’s easier to clean; the spray nozzle on my sink blasts away stuck-on bits. A few quick shakes, and it’s basically dry.

When shopping for new strainers, be sure that the wire mesh is durable — look for “304 stainless steel” rather than “201.” (The 304 stuff contains [a higher percentage of chromium](https://www.everich.com/stainless-steel-304-vs-201-what-is-the-difference-between-the-two/), which is sturdier and less resistant to rust.)

# How to make juice at home without a juicer

Warning: time is required.

Credit:

![Courtney Campbell](https://images.reviewed.com/fit-in/120x120/filters:strip_icc():strip_exif():no_upscale():format(webp):quality(65)/1541787456000/Courtney-Campbell-Headshot.jpg)

**Written by** **[Courtney Campbell](https://www.reviewed.com/authors/courtney-campbell)**

March 20, 2018

Products are chosen independently by our editors. Purchases made through our links may earn us a commission.

The juice craze is real, people. From hearing about your neighbor’s latest attempt at a juice cleanse to that fancy juice bar opening down the street, juice is popping up everywhere. But it can be expensive—literally, it seems like your only options is to spend $5 on a pre-made juice or shell out $300 for [a good juicer](https://www.reviewed.com/home-outdoors/best-right-now/the-best-juicers).

Juices are loaded with vitamins and minerals as well as detoxifying properties, so it seems a little unfair for those of us on a budget. Thankfully, there's a way to create delicious and nutritious juice using kitchen products you probably already have. It may be more time-consuming (and messier) than a juicer, but you can get homemade juice without taking out a loan. It might just be worth the effort.

**Here’s what you’ll need:**

* [A strong blender](https://r.bttn.io?btn_ref=org-4e216a16a82e7346&btn_url=http%3A%2F%2Famzn.to%2F2FYbbmE)
* A spatula
* [A fine mesh strainer](https://r.bttn.io?btn_ref=org-4e216a16a82e7346&btn_url=http%3A%2F%2Famzn.to%2F2GMRxeF)
* A bowl
* Fruits and veggies for juicing
* [A sturdy cutting board](https://r.bttn.io?btn_ref=org-4e216a16a82e7346&btn_url=http%3A%2F%2Famzn.to%2F2u24Eps)
* [A good chef’s knife](https://r.bttn.io?btn_ref=org-4e216a16a82e7346&btn_url=http%3A%2F%2Famzn.to%2F2pqq0rI)

## Step 1: Prepare your produce

![Cutting Vegetables](https://images.reviewed.com/fit-in/792x0/filters:strip_icc():strip_exif():no_upscale():format(webp):quality(65)/attachment/1b558ee047b842a4/TotallyBamboo.jpg)


Credit:
Reviewed / Jackson Ruckar

Wash all the fruits and veggies you plan on using and then chop them into chunks using [a sharp chef's knife](https://r.bttn.io?btn_ref=org-4e216a16a82e7346&btn_url=http%3A%2F%2Famzn.to%2F2pqq0rI) and [a cutting board](https://r.bttn.io?btn_ref=org-4e216a16a82e7346&btn_url=http%3A%2F%2Famzn.to%2F2u24Eps) that won't slide around. Make sure you remove and rinds or pits from the produce—you do not want those bitter flavors in your juice (yuck!). Feel free to leave the skin on most other produce including apples, carrots, and beets, as long as you’re sure you got all the dirt off. These are often loaded with nutrients!

## Step 2: Blend, baby, blend

![Breville Blender](https://images.reviewed.com/fit-in/792x0/filters:strip_icc():strip_exif():no_upscale():format(webp):quality(65)/attachment/b5dd79f23f244ca4/Breville_Boss_Super_Blender.jpg)


Credit:
Reviewed / Kyle Looney

Load your ingredients into the blender. To ensure optimal blending, make sure the juicier produce goes in first, like citrus, watermelon, and cucumbers, followed by greens and tougher vegetables. Then get to blending.

Since most juices require tougher produce like beets, carrot, and kale, you might want to use a high-powered blender—[like our favorite](https://r.bttn.io?btn_ref=org-4e216a16a82e7346&btn_url=http%3A%2F%2Famzn.to%2F2FYbbmE). If your mixture is very thick, you can add water or lemon juice, or give it a stir to help it along.

## Step 3: Strain away

Once the ingredients are blended, it should look more like a watery smoothie than juice. But do not fear, you won't be drinking all of that pulp! You’re going to want to pour the mixture over [a mesh strainer](https://r.bttn.io?btn_ref=org-4e216a16a82e7346&btn_url=http%3A%2F%2Famzn.to%2F2GMRxeF) set on top of a bowl to strain the liquid. Some of the juice will drip through on its own. You will also want to press the pulp down with a spatula to ensure you get every last drop.

## Step 4: Enjoy!

After all that hard work, it’s time to enjoy your labor of love. You can compost the pulp, save it for recipes like vegetable stock, or mix it in with cream cheese for a fun spread.

While summer is a great time for plants in your garden to thrive, it's also the perfect breeding ground for hungry aphids and other pests.

As quickly as the sun begins to shine, the aphids descend upon your yard, from vegetable patches to rose bushes – and they can become a serious problem.

Causing damage and sucking plant sap from your hard-grown crops can even lead to killing them, if left untreated.

[Watch full video here:](https://www.tomsguide.com/home/gardening/gardeners-urged-to-use-mushrooms-in-the-yard-this-summer-this-hack-will-banish-aphids-in-minutes)

Fortunately, this expert hack from [SporeBuddies](https://sporebuddies.com/) means getting rid of aphids doesn't have to cost you a lot of cash and it's incredibly easy.

The answer? Mushrooms. According to mushroom expert Waine Delaney, "Many edible mushrooms, like shiitake and oyster, contain certain bioactive compounds that are antifungal, antimicrobial, and insect-repelling".

When I first heard about making a mushroom spray, I thought it sounded pretty... tasty. For insects though, mushrooms "contain enzymes, phenolics, and bitter-tasting compounds that repel pests like slugs and snails".

## Why mushrooms can repel aphids

![Aphids on a rose bud](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/jqRahXXsUDc6daQw5H66cY.jpg)

(Image credit: Shutterstock)

As briefly explained, there's certain features of a mushroom that pests like aphids, slugs and snails *hate*. But, not all mushrooms.

Certain fungi can be transformed into a natural spray that'll deter aphids because, according to Delaney: "when sprayed onto a plants surface and the surrounding soil, the surface residue and unfamiliar scent confuses them, and signals that the plant is inedible". (I wish someone would do this on chocolate for me).

He explains that you may even find specific fungi growing in your backyard, called entomopathogenic mushrooms. 'Entomo' meaning insect and 'pathogenic' meaning disease and it's these mushrooms that can kill insects biologically, rather than opting for a chemical pest solution.

What's even better, Delaney explains: "Though they are able to control pests, they do not harm insects that are beneficial – such as bees, butterflies, or ladybirds – and they are completely safe for humans, pets, and birds."

Fortunately, you can also pick these mushrooms up at your local garden center or online. And you may already have some at home as everyday edible mushrooms found in your local grocery store will also work.

Oyster, shiitake, button or white mushrooms and king oyster mushrooms can all act as effective pest repellents.

![Chopping mushrooms](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/SPEQgav7JJ6DHdwATEZ8Xi.jpg)

(Image credit: Shutterstock)

Oyster mushrooms are specifically good for targeting slugs, snails, aphids and greenfly as they "contain enzymes and toxins that can digest soft-bodied pests and small insects".

Shiitake mushrooms are best for caterpillars, aphids and greenfly, thanks to their antimicrobial properties.

Button or white mushrooms target greenfly and aphids, but work better as a base or filler for a homemade spray, used alongside other mushrooms to create a stronger deterrent.

And, king oyster mushrooms are for your garden slugs and snails as they repel soft-bodied pests with their nematode-trapping toxins.

## Make your own spray

Whichever mushrooms you opt for, you'll need a blender (and we'd recommend some of the [best blenders](https://www.tomsguide.com/best-picks/best-blenders) on the market right now), cheesecloth or fine mesh strainer, a jug, and a spray bottle.

Plus, if you want to bulk out your natural pest repellent with some additional properties, there's some extras you can use like peppermint oil, rosemary, garlic extract or neem oil.

Here's how you make a natural mushroom spray for your garden:

* Place your mushrooms in a blender or food processor with water
* Blend until smooth
* Strain the mixture through a cheesecloth or fine mesh strainer into a jug to remove lumps
* Here, you can add extras, if you wish
* Pour the mixture into a spray bottle, adding more water if required
* Shake well before use
* Spray directly onto the leaves, stems and bases of your plants
* Repeat every few days, or if it rains

![Slug eating its way through a basil leaf](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/XrZBsLzzJVH6m6xi9CK2R.jpg)

(Image credit: Shutterstock)

While mushrooms will deal with your aphid problem, they'll also deal with other pests like slugs, snails, greenflies, whiteflies, caterpillars, and beetle larvae.

So, even if aphids aren't your biggest problem in the garden, your natural mushroom spray can do the work to deter other pests at the same time.

And, if you've bought a multipack of spray bottles, there's no reason you can't arm yourself with a [vinegar spray to rid your home of an ant problem](https://www.tomsguide.com/home/experts-say-you-should-spray-vinegar-outside-your-front-door-this-summer-heres-why) or a [garlic spray for natural pest control](https://www.tomsguide.com/home/outdoors/gardeners-urged-to-use-garlic-in-their-yards-experts-share-reasons-why).

It has the same mesh filter-style lid as the Hiware models, filtering loose-leaf tea like a champ with no floating bits in your drink.

The **Artcome** handle conducted a fair amount of heat when boiling water on the stove. It wasn't enough to require a potholder, but something to remember while heating. The mouth of the pitcher just barely fits a hand, so we suggest anyone with large hands use the brush just to be safe. There’s something refreshingly simple about brewing a cup or two of coffee in a French-press or pour-over coffee maker. Both styles can produce excellent coffee in a matter of minutes, because you need to heat only the amount of water you’ll use. That shorter brew time also means that coffee tends to be hotter than from a large, drip coffee maker, which often takes more than 10 minutes to make a pot.

If you’re not a frequent coffee drinker, keeping a French-press or pour-over coffee maker stashed in the cupboard is the perfect way to make the occasional cup without dedicating a large section of countertop to an appliance you’ll seldom use.

Though virtually all of the French presses and pour-over coffee makers that Consumer Reports tested make a good cup of coffee, they varied in their ease of use, with the best of the bunch keeping hands safely away from hot surfaces and proving easy to clean. Top-performing French presses varied in the quality of their permanent mesh filters, which is the only line of defense against grounds that can otherwise end up in your cup. Below, a selection of top manual coffee makers from our most recent tests.

## French-Press Coffee Makers

**Frieling Insulated Brushed Stainless Steel, $124.99**  
 With a price that would seem steep on even the best electric brewer, the Frieling topped our test of French-press models in large part because of its insulated, stainless steel design. That helped it keep coffee hot and hands cool, and its double-layer mesh strainer had the smallest openings of any model reviewed, helping it keep grounds from slipping through into brewed coffee. But unlike glass models, you can’t see how much coffee is left in the carafe.

**Bodum 8-Cup Chambord, $49.99**  
 It looks like glass, but the Chambord is actually outfitted with what Bodum describes as a shatter-resistant, BPA-free SAN plastic carafe. Indeed, the carafe did resist shattering when we dropped it—a clear advantage over glass options—though it still fractured at the point where it hit the floor.

**Bonjour 8-Cup Monet, $39.99**  
 This classically designed press has a standard glass carafe wrapped in stainless steel. Clear sides let you see exactly how much is left to pour but don’t do much to keep coffee hot—or protect hands. The wide handle allows you to easily grip and pour without getting too close to the hot sides.

**Bodum Brazil 8-Cup, $17.99**  
 It’s tough to beat the price on this simple press, which has a plastic lid, base, and handle surrounding the glass carafe. It was as easy to use as models costing twice as much, but the small handle keeps hands close to the hot glass sides, so you’ll need to use a little caution when pouring.

## Pour-Over Coffee Makers

**Melitta 2- to 6-Cup Pour-Over Coffee Brewer, $12.99**  
 For simple, straightforward brewing, the Melitta is a solid choice. A plastic cone sits atop the glass carafe and features a large finger ring, eliminating the need to get hands too close to hot surfaces. The carafe has a wide neck and is easily cleaned by hand, and the unit relies on disposable filters that do a good job capturing grounds.

**Bodum Pour Over 11571-01 with Permanent Filter, $29.99**  
 The narrow neck on the Bodum lends itself to the handsome, hourglass-inspired design. Unfortunately, that same narrow neck makes this model difficult to clean. A rubber sleeve wraps the carafe to protect fingers while pouring, but it’s not large enough to protect an entire hand. The neck has a permanent filter, which eliminates the need for disposable paper filters, though some fine grounds can sneak through.
